the expansion of the carbon market in the form of plantation forestry is associated with the following types of carbon violence: (1) the violence of displacement, (2) the violence of land alienation, (3) the violence of dispossession, (4) the violence of environmental destruction and (5) the violence of the market itself.
the expansion of plantation forestry carbon markets in Uganda is associated with a new form of ‘carbon violence’.
plantation forestry in Uganda is associated with a range of forms of violence.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the expansion of carbon markets, the role of plantation forestry and the impacts on local communities.
the violence of the carbon economy, and the violence that is carbon.
the violence of carbon markets and the new carbon violence.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
plantation forestry carbon markets in Uganda are a form of ‘carbon violence’.
the plantation forestry carbon market is a form of violence against the people of Uganda.
plantation forestry carbon market expansion is a form of ‘carbon violence’ in Uganda, and elsewhere.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
carbon markets are not only failing to address global warming, but they are also contributing to a new form of ‘carbon violence’ that threatens to further undermine local livelihoods.
the plantation forestry sector is a key driver of carbon violence, with the carbon economy being used to justify and legitimate this violence.
the expansion of the plantation forestry sector in Uganda, as part of the global carbon market, is associated with multiple and diverse forms of violence.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the expansion of carbon markets and plantation forestry is not a benign process.
plantation forestry carbon markets are not the ‘win-win-win’ scenario they are often presented as, but rather represent an extension of structural violence, and are a form of carbon violence.
the expansion of the plantation forestry industry in Uganda is not a neutral or benign process; rather, it is a process of carbon violence.
